terms.definition: Code that works with any type, so you write it once instead of once for each type.
terms.example: We made the cache generic, so it can store images, users, or anything else.

terms.definition: A placeholder name, like T, for a type that is filled in later when the code is used.
terms.example: In this function, T is the type parameter, and it becomes Int when we pass in numbers.

terms.definition: A rule that limits a generic to types that meet a requirement, such as conforming to a protocol.
terms.example: I added a generic constraint so the function only accepts types that are Equatable.

Hi everyone! Today we are talking about generics in Swift.

Today's 3 terms
Generic: code that works with any type, so you write it once.
Type Parameter: a placeholder name, like T, for a type that is filled in later.
Generic Constraint: a rule that limits a generic to types that meet a requirement.

Each example is read twice, normal speed and then slow, so you can say it out loud with me.

dialogue.title: Tech debt Friday: three caches, one idea

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is tech debt Friday. Look, we have ImageCache, UserCache, and PostCache.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: They are almost the same code. Only the stored type is different.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: This is a job for generics. We write the cache once, for any type.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So a generic cache can store images, users, or anything else.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. We write Cache with angle brackets and a name inside, like Value.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What is that name called again?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It is the type parameter. It is only a placeholder for a type that is filled in later.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So when I write Cache of String, the type parameter becomes String.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. Now we have one generic type instead of three copies.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Let me try a function too. I want to check if two values are the same.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Go ahead.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I wrote a generic function that compares a and b. But Xcode shows an error on the equals sign.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Of course. Not every type can be compared. Swift does not know your type parameter supports it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So I need to say the type must be Equatable.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, that is a generic constraint. You write a colon after the type parameter.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: With the generic constraint, the function only accepts types that are Equatable.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: And a generic constraint gives a clear error when someone passes the wrong type.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Nice. Now it builds. One generic, one type parameter, one generic constraint.
We made the cache generic, so it stores any type.
